name: Hydrogen combustion
note: Releases 286 kJ/mol H₂O; used in hydrogen fuel cells and rocket engines (e.g. Space Shuttle main engines).

name: Methane combustion
note: The main reaction burning natural gas for heat and power.

name: Propane combustion
note: Powers gas grills, camp stoves and some heaters.

name: Octane combustion (gasoline)
note: Idealized complete combustion of a major gasoline component in an engine.

name: Carbon combustion (complete)
note: Complete combustion with sufficient oxygen — coal, charcoal.

name: Carbon combustion (incomplete)
note: Limited oxygen produces toxic carbon monoxide instead of CO₂ — the danger in poorly ventilated fires.

name: Carbon monoxide combustion
note: CO itself is flammable and burns with a blue flame to complete combustion.

name: Sulfur combustion
note: A precursor step to acid rain and to industrial sulfuric acid production.

name: Magnesium combustion
note: Burns with a brilliant white light — used historically in flash photography and still in flares/fireworks.

name: Magnesium burning in CO₂
note: Magnesium is reactive enough to strip oxygen from CO₂ — this is why CO₂ extinguishers can't put out a magnesium fire.

name: Hydrogen sulfide combustion
note: H₂S ('rotten egg gas') is itself flammable and toxic.

name: Cellular respiration (net)
note: The overall equation for how your cells release energy from glucose — the real pathway is dozens of enzyme steps.

name: Photosynthesis (net)
note: The reverse of respiration, driven by light energy in chloroplasts; source of nearly all atmospheric O₂.

name: Haber process (ammonia synthesis)
note: Industrial fixation of nitrogen for fertilizer, run at high pressure/temperature over an iron catalyst — feeds roughly half the world's population.

name: Aluminum oxidation
note: Forms the thin, tough oxide layer that protects aluminum from further corrosion.

name: Iron oxidation (rust, simplified)
note: Real rusting also needs water and is more complex, but this net equation captures the overall change.

name: Sodium chloride formation
note: A soft, dangerously reactive metal and a toxic gas combine into ordinary table salt.

name: Hydrogen chloride formation
note: Proceeds explosively in bright light via a radical chain reaction.

name: Slaking lime
note: Strongly exothermic — used in cement/mortar and can scald if handled carelessly.

name: Sodium oxide + water
note: Forms caustic sodium hydroxide (lye).

name: Carbonic acid formation
note: Why soda water is acidic and fizzy, and a key step in ocean acidification.

name: Sulfuric acid formation
note: Net final step of the industrial Contact Process for the world's most-produced industrial chemical. (In practice SO₃ is absorbed into concentrated H₂SO₄ first — adding it straight to water makes a corrosive acid mist.)

name: Sulfur trioxide formation (Contact process)
note: Catalyzed by vanadium(V) oxide industrially; also happens slowly in polluted air as acid rain forms.

name: Nitric oxide formation
note: Needs very high temperature (like a lightning bolt or a car engine) since N₂'s triple bond is so strong.

name: Nitrogen dioxide formation
note: NO reacts spontaneously with air; NO₂ is the reddish-brown gas behind urban smog.

name: Xenon tetrafluoride
note: Proof that 'inert' noble gases can bond — synthesized in 1962, overturning the assumption they never react.

name: Hydrogen peroxide decomposition
note: Catalyzed by the enzyme catalase in blood/cells (the fizz on a cut) or by manganese dioxide.

name: Limestone calcination
note: Roasting limestone to make quicklime — one of the oldest industrial chemical reactions, and a major CO₂ source from cement making.

name: Potassium chlorate decomposition
note: Catalyzed by MnO₂; a classic way to generate oxygen in the lab. Aircraft and submarine 'oxygen candles' use the closely related sodium chlorate.

name: Sodium bicarbonate decomposition
note: Baking soda breaking down with heat — part of how baked goods rise.

name: Silver bromide photolysis
note: Light splitting silver bromide into metallic silver is the basis of traditional photographic film.

name: Electrolysis of water
note: The reverse of hydrogen combustion — driven by electrical energy instead of releasing it; a route to 'green' hydrogen.

name: Zinc + hydrochloric acid
note: A classic lab demonstration of a reactive metal displacing hydrogen from acid.

name: Iron + copper sulfate
note: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it — a nail dipped in blue copper sulfate solution turns copper-coated.

name: Copper + silver nitrate ('silver tree')
note: Silver crystals visibly grow on the copper wire as it dissolves — a striking classroom demo.

name: Sodium + water
note: Vigorous and often flame-producing as the released hydrogen ignites.

name: Potassium + water
note: More violent than sodium — reactivity increases going down Group 1.

name: Calcium + water
note: Milder and slower than the alkali metals, consistent with alkaline-earth metals' lower reactivity.

name: Aluminum + sulfuric acid
note: Aluminum's protective oxide layer must first be breached before this proceeds readily.

name: Chlorine displaces bromine
note: Reactivity falls going down Group 17, so a lighter halogen displaces a heavier one from its salt.

name: Bromine displaces iodine
note: Same trend one step further down the halogen group.

name: Fluorine displaces chlorine
note: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen — it displaces every other halogen from their salts (dry or molten; in water, fluorine attacks the water itself).

name: Silver chloride precipitation
note: The classic qualitative test for chloride ions — a white precipitate forms instantly.

name: Barium sulfate precipitation
note: BaSO₄'s extreme insolubility is why it's used (safely) as an X-ray contrast agent despite barium's toxicity.

name: Lead iodide precipitation ('golden rain')
note: Forms a brilliant yellow precipitate — a favorite visual chemistry demonstration.

name: Limewater test for CO₂
note: Limewater turning cloudy is the standard school test confirming a gas is carbon dioxide.

name: Neutralization (HCl + NaOH)
note: The textbook strong acid + strong base neutralization, producing table salt and water.

name: Neutralization (H₂SO₄ + KOH)
note: A diprotic acid needs two bases to fully neutralize.

name: Baking soda volcano
note: Vinegar + baking soda — the CO₂ bubbles are the 'eruption' in the classic science-fair volcano. The reaction is slightly endothermic: the mixture gets cooler.

name: Thermite reaction
note: Extremely exothermic — reaches ~2500 °C, molten iron pours out. Used for welding railway rails.
